newsitem.title: CANADA: Chretien to head for smooth meeting with Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Chretien to head for smooth meeting with Clinton.

text.p: In the absence of any major disputes, Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien's first official visit to Washington next week will deal mostly with issues such as trans-border pollution and clearing passengers through Vancouver airport, officials said.
"The problem (for journalists) is there are not too many problems. There is no big hole in our relationship that needs to be patched," a Chretien aide said on Thursday.
"It's hard to find very many disagreements," echoed a senior U.S. official, noting Chretien and U.S. President Bill Clinton get along well.
Chretien, who will fly to Washington on Monday, will hold 70 minutes of talks with Clinton and attend a White House dinner on Tuesday before flying back to Ottawa on Wednesday.
Officials on both sides said the leaders certainly would touch on their thorniest dispute, Washington's anti-Castro Helms-Burton Act.
Chretien will again press Clinton to get rid of the bill, which punishes some companies in third countries that do business in Cuba, or at least to continue to suspend a key provision in the bill.
In talks with congressional leaders, he will also press Washington to agree on a treaty to conserve Pacific salmon.
Also on the agenda is Canada's desire for the United States to join its efforts to ban land mines globally.

But to a large extent, the U.S. official said, the visit will be designed to preserve the world's richest bilateral relationship, involving a billion dollars a day in trade and 200 million visitors crossing the border each year.
"To a certain extent they'll obviously be celebrating (that relationship)," he said.

Clinton and his wife Hillary paid an official visit to Ottawa in February 1995, and the two leaders have met many times in other forums, but this will be the first official visit by Chretien since taking office in late 1993.
Some Canadian commentators suggested Chretien timed the visit to look prime ministerial ahead of general elections he is expected to call for June or October. Chretien's camp dismisses that argument.
Residents on both sides of the border probably will be most directly affected by environmental agreements to be signed by ministers of the two countries.
One agreement, a Canadian official said, would be to develop a joint plan of action to cut down on trans-border smog -- especially low-level ozone and small particles.

He said the idea would be for cuts on the order of 50 percent or more, although no targets would be set in next week's agreement. Canada says more than half the smog in the central Ontario-Quebec border area comes from the United States.
A second pact would provide for the "virtual elimination" from the Great Lakes of toxic substances like PCBs and dioxins.
A third agreement will pledge work on protecting endangered species like grizzly bears that cross the border.

Another deal, symbolic of the goal to improve trans-border flows, will provide for Asian passengers transiting through Vancouver airport to the United States to go directly through U.S. customs in Vancouver and avoid Canadian customs.
